newsitem.title: USA: Republicans may have trouble in Southern House races.
newsitem.headline: Republicans may have trouble in Southern House races.

text.p: Republicans can count on adding only a handful of House seats in the South, a region they had once hoped would hand them a windfall in the November election, analysts say.
Democrats need to win back 20 seats to take control of the House, where Republicans hold a 235-198 advantage.

Crucial to the outcome is the South, and especially 17 "open" seats scattered across 11 states from Texas to Virginia, where retiring incumbent Democrats have left their party vulnerable to Republican incursion.

Early in the year, Republicans had been expected to add up to a dozen seats, thanks to an historic shift of the conservative Southern electorate away from its allegiance to Democrats. But now, with just six weeks left in the campaign, analysts said the odds of a widespread Republican victory are suddenly running low.

"I'd expect the Republicans to pick up between one and five House seats in the South -- five if it's a good election for them generally. At the moment, it doesn't look as though they'll do that well," said Merle Black, a leading expert on Southern politics at Emory University in Atlanta.

Big gains for Southern Republicans in November would make up for potential party losses elsewhere, particulary defeats of vulnerable Republicans who won by narrow margins in the 1994 Republican landslide in the Northeast, Midwest and West.
Analysts say a half dozen new Southern Republican seats in the House would be enough to foil Democratic ambitions. But Republicans face some daunting hurdles.

"I think you'd want to see a Republican presidential candidate doing a little better than Bob Dole is doing now. He certainly isn't going to provide much assistance to these congressional candidates," said political scientist Charles Bullock at the University of Georgia.

Democrats are making effective use of the public apprehension stirred by House Speaker Newt Gingrich and some of his more controversial actions, such as shutting down the government in a confrontation with President Clinton over balancing the budget.

"Most of the Democrats running for open seats are running as moderate to conservative Democrats. They're running as 'reasonable' conservatives as opposed to 'extremist' conservatives in the Republican Party," said Black.

A good example is Texas Democrat Jim Turner, who is expected to defeat Republican Brian Babin in the 2nd district, a largely rural area that has been represented for years by retiring Democrat Charlie Wilson.
A long-time state legislator, Turner boasts a fairly conservative record by national standards on issues like building prisons to combating crime and balancing the budget.

"But it's very easy to have the middle ground when you're running against a guy who was a delegate to a state Republican convention that advocated the abolition of the minimum wage," said Scott Bates, Turner's campaign manager.

"In 1995, the Gingrich budget proposed some radical cuts that would have hurt the people of east Texas, and they know it," he said. "And our opponent is on record as saying he would have supported that budget."

A few Democrats who were unseated by the anti-incumbent fever of 1994 also are expected to return to office. The list includes David Price, who lost North Carolina's 4th district by a slim margin despite its large Democratic leaning.

Analysts say the surest bet for Republicans is Mississippi's 3rd Congressional District, where polls show a former aide to Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott leading his Democratic opponent by 25 percent. Republicans also could do well in the 3rd and 4th districts of Alabama, as well as in the 1st, 2nd and 5th in Texas.
Republicans say voters have yet to start paying attention to congressional races, which often heat up only in the final two weeks of the campaign.

"As the public begins to focus on the congressional races, they're going to realise the significant accomplishments that the Republican-controlled Congress has made," said Craig Veith, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee in Washington.
